title: Ultrasonic jet bat deterrent system advancement
abstract:
General Electric Renewable Energy (GE) and the Department of Energy (DOE) worked to develop a project with an objective to increase confidence in acoustic ultrasonic bat deterrent technologies in wind turbines, by mitigating stakeholder investment risks that currently hinder the adoption of deterrent technologies. Many wind turbine sites utilize a bat conservation plan that curtail wind turbines and stop energy production. Curtailment is a known bat impact mitigation solution that has an history of environmental regulatory acceptance. To help support a solution that allows for simultaneous bat conservation and energy production with regulatory acceptance of acoustic bat deterrents, GE proposed a study to compare four treatments: control (no curtailment or deterrent), deterrent only, deterrent plus curtailment, and curtailment only. The concept was to provide a direct comparison of bat deterrent and curtailment effectiveness within the same wind farm and bat migration season. This comparison was intended to advocate for the adoption of bat deterrents with a large-scale field study by addressing customer concerns on regulatory acceptance of deterrents. The study was to be hosted at a forested habitat site during a bat migration season, by Stony Creek Energy, LLC (SCE), the owner of the Orangeville Wind Farm (OWF) in the state of New York. Included was a behavioral study plan with two turbines to monitor bat flight paths with thermal imaging cameras.
The proposed program was planned to take place over two budget periods, which included the development of the research study design and execution of a field study to measure and compare effectiveness. The initial research study plan included approximately 40 wind turbines with 60meter (m) radius test plots. The research study plan was submitted for a DOE hosted peer review in September 2019. To account for a wind speed bias, the peer review team desired 90-m or greater plot sizes to account for bat carcasses landing at an increased distance from the wind turbine base at high wind speeds. Plot searches involve inspecting the entire searchable area of each test wind turbine plot, the increased plot size caused a marked increase in program cost. DOE and GE mutually agreed that the budget for the increased size of the ground searches to evaluate treatment efficacy, were more important than the thermal imaging behavioral study, as a result the behavioral study was mutually removed from the program in 2019.
With support from the DOE and peer reviewers, the team continued to evolve the research study plan. For acceptance of the research study plan, statistical simulations needed to demonstrate the power to detect the effectiveness of the deterrent. A key issue was the low number of expected bat fatalities at the selected wind site resulted in a small sample size, which, when combined with budget ceilings and the number of turbines available for the study, resulted in insufficient power to detect differences among treatments. Additional revisions of the research study plan were not able to resolve peer reviewer concerns with the wind speed bias and proposed statistical assumptions. The estimated bat activity, available turbines, and study plots, the simulation studies indicated that the four-treatment proposal (as listed above) and any threetreatment variations of the studies would be statistically inconclusive regarding treatment effectiveness. After multiple revisions to improve methods and expand the study parameters within the budget identified at award, the program goals and objectives could not be met in a manner that would satisfy the intent of the original DOE Funding Opportunity Announcement (FOA) and GE’s original proposal. As a result, the DOE and GE came to an agreement to mutually terminate the program during Budget Period 1 (BP1) in May 2021, prior to the execution of any field work.

## **EXECUTIVE SUMMARY**

General Electric Renewable Energy (GE) and the Department of Energy (DOE) worked to develop a project with an objective to increase confidence in acoustic ultrasonic bat deterrent technologies in wind turbines, by mitigating stakeholder investment risks that currently hinder the adoption of deterrent technologies. Many wind turbine sites utilize a bat conservation plan that curtail wind turbines and stop energy production.  Curtailment is a known bat impact mitigation solution that has an history of environmental regulatory acceptance.  To help support a solution that allows for simultaneous bat conservation and energy production with regulatory acceptance of acoustic bat deterrents, GE proposed a study to compare four treatments: control (no curtailment or deterrent), deterrent only, deterrent plus curtailment, and curtailment only.  The concept was to provide a direct comparison of bat deterrent and curtailment effectiveness within the same wind farm and bat migration season.  This comparison was intended to advocate for the adoption of bat deterrents with a large-scale field study by addressing customer concerns on regulatory acceptance of deterrents. The study was to be hosted at a forested habitat site during a bat migration season, by Stony Creek Energy, LLC (SCE), the owner of the Orangeville Wind Farm (OWF) in the state of New York.  Included was a behavioral study plan with two turbines to monitor bat flight paths with thermal imaging cameras.

The proposed program was planned to take place over two budget periods, which included the development of the research study design and execution of a field study to measure and compare effectiveness. The initial research study plan included approximately 40 wind turbines with 60meter (m) radius test plots. The research study plan was submitted for a DOE hosted peer review in September 2019.  To account for a wind speed bias, the peer review team desired 90-m or greater plot sizes to account for bat carcasses landing at an increased distance from the wind turbine base at high wind speeds. Plot searches involve inspecting the entire searchable area of each test wind turbine plot, the increased plot size caused a marked increase in program cost. DOE and GE mutually agreed that the budget for the increased size of the ground searches to evaluate treatment efficacy, were more important than the thermal imaging behavioral study, as a result the behavioral study was mutually removed from the program in 2019.

With support from the DOE and peer reviewers, the team continued to evolve the research study plan.  For acceptance of the research study plan, statistical simulations needed to demonstrate the power to detect the effectiveness of the deterrent.  A key issue was the low number of expected bat fatalities at the selected wind site resulted in a small sample size, which, when combined with budget ceilings and the number of turbines available for the study, resulted in insufficient power to detect differences among treatments. Additional revisions of the research study plan were not able to resolve peer reviewer concerns with the wind speed bias and proposed statistical assumptions.  The estimated bat activity, available turbines, and study plots, the simulation studies indicated that the four-treatment proposal (as listed above) and any threetreatment variations of the studies would be statistically inconclusive regarding treatment effectiveness.  After multiple revisions to improve methods and expand the study parameters within the budget identified at award, the program goals and objectives could not be met in a manner that would satisfy the intent of the original DOE Funding Opportunity Announcement (FOA) and GE’s original proposal.  As a result, the DOE and GE came to an agreement to mutually terminate the program during Budget Period 1 (BP1) in May 2021, prior to the execution of any field work.

## **1 ACCOMPLISHMENTS**

## **1.1 Project Goals and Objectives**

In 2018, GE Renewables conducted customer and regulator outreach to obtain input to further the commercialization of bat deterrents in the wind industry. The feedback obtained included apprehension on making an investment risk on all bat deterrents due to: 1) Lack of validation of acoustic deterrent effectiveness results, 2) Unknown regulatory agency acceptance of deterrents as a fatality avoidance and minimization strategy, 3) Data supporting deterrent performance in multiple habitats with multiple species assemblages, 4) Effectiveness of bat deterrents when deployed over an entire wind farm and 5) How does the relative effectiveness of deterrence vs. curtailment compare (such a comparison would allow stakeholders to determine if deterrence is a cost-effective, acceptable conservation tool to be used in lieu of or in conjunction with curtailment). To address stakeholder concerns and to follow-up on results from GE’s previous studies, more research is desired, and is the basis for this study.

The project objective was to increase stakeholder confidence  of acoustic ultrasonic bat deterrent technologies in wind turbines by mitigating the stakeholder investment risks that limit the adoption of deterrent technologies. GE proposed to mitigate identified stakeholder risks by answering these five questions to advocate for the adoption of bat deterrents with a large-scale field study. The study was to be hosted by SCE at the OWF in New York, utilizing approximately 40 wind turbines, and bat behavioral studies at two turbines, at a forested habitat site during the 2020 bat migration season.

## **1.2 Technical Approach and Accomplishments Summary**

The technical approach included the following research activities and accomplishments.

Completion of a research study plan (Milestones 1.1.1 and 1.2.1) and DOE approval of the final research study plan (Milestone 1.2.2). In September 2019, GE submitted the first draft of their study design, developed by Dr. John Skalski.  Over the course of the study design per review Dr. Skalski retired and was replaced by Dr. Patrick Sullivan, who worked with Dr. Leslie New to develop a revised study design to address feedback from the DOE peer review team. This process included conducting various simulation studies to attend to reviewer concerns. Simulation study results suggested that the program goals could not be met at the OWF site within the funded budget.

## **2 Project Activities**

The overall Project Plan with Milestones, Schedule, and Comments are shown in Table 3.

## **2.1 Research Study Plan Development (Tasks 1.1 and 1.2)**

GE’s original statistician, Dr. John Skalski, retired in the fall of 2019, Dr. Patrick Sullivan was hired to continue the program, who was then Chairman of the Department of Natural Resources at Cornell University. Due to insurance requirements, Dr. Sullivan was contracted by GE via Shoener Environmental. Dr. Sullivan retired in December 2020 and continued working on this program at GE’s request. In the fall of 2020, Shoener Environmental was purchased by TRC Companies,

requiring new contracts to be established with TRC. Dr. Sullivan’s retirement from Cornell at the end of 2020 also necessitated that his contract be revised.

In September 2020, the DOE supported GE to augment the statistical team with a statistician with wind-wildlife experience to help attend with peer review concerns.  With the support of the DOE, GE added Dr. Leslie New, an assistant professor at Washington State University (WSU), to the team. A contract with WSU was signed to obtain Dr. Leslie New’s services in February 2021. The contract signed between WSU and GE provided a statement of work for Dr. New to assist GE in supporting a comment response matrix to address peer review concerns and finalize the study plan.  Dr. New withdrew from the project at the end of May 2021, due to a change in personal circumstance.

## **2.2 Activities and Accomplishments**

Milestone 1.1.1 – Completion of a draft research study plan for methods peer review, and Milestone 1.2.1 - Completion of revised research study plan in response to the peer review

The original research study plan was submitted to DOE in September 2019. After which, the project team evolved the research study plan with two additional revisions from July 2019 through May 2021. Below is a summary list of each revision:

1. Randomized block design, submitted 23 Sept. 2019, developed with Dr. John Skalski a. In addition, a synopsis submitted for clarification on 7 Dec 2019

2. Repeated measures design utilizing a Generalized linear mixed-effects (GLMM) model, submitted on 17 June 2020, developed with Dr. Patrick Sullivan

3. Expansion of the repeated measures design with wind turbines randomized across treatment and plot size configuration with binning of wind speeds, developed with Dr. Patrick Sullivan and Dr. Leslie New

   - a. In addition, a direct comparison of repeated measures to random block designs, developed by Dr. Leslie New and Jeff Mintz.

## **2.3 First version of the research study plan - Randomized block design**

The randomized block design research study plan was proposed to have 40 study wind turbines to be randomly selected from the 58-wind turbine project.

The randomized block design was proposed to evaluate four treatments. The test blocks proposed in three-day durations. Within a block, available turbines were randomly assigned to the four treatments of at a rate of ten turbines per treatment. The four treatments would be as follows:

1. deterrent off, factory wind speed cut-in 3.5 m/s (control, CNDN),

2. deterrent on, cut-in 3.5 m/s (CNDY),

3. deterrent on, cut-in increased to 5.0 m/s (CYDY),

4. deterrent off, cut-in increased to 6.9 m/s (CYDN).

Each test block was proposed to last for three days, then the four treatments would be rerandomized to the forty turbines and a new test block would be performed. The study anticipated performing 26 test blocks over the course of the study. To help assure the treatments were

spatially distributed evenly but randomly across the forty available test turbines, assignment of the treatments was based on a generalized random tessellation spatially balanced sampling design.

The four treatments were proposed to allow meaningful tests of contrast to be performed consistent with the stated study goals:

- a) the initial test would compare the control condition (CNDN) to the other three treatments to test for increased deterrence effect,

- b) compare effectiveness of the deterrent verses higher cut-in speed (i.e., CNDY vs. CYDN),

- c) compare alternative cut-in speeds in the absence of the deterrent (i.e., CNDN vs. CYDN),

- d) compare alternative maximum avoidance treatments (i.e., CYDY vs. CYDN).

Test of the hypotheses would be at α = 0.10, 1-tailed when applicable.  Alternatively, the contrast “d” should be 2-tailed because directionality of the contrast under the alternative hypothesis is not obvious. As anticipated, a total of 26 three-day test blocks were proposed to be performed. The experiment was expected to produce a total of 26 x 4 = 104 estimates of bat mortality upon which the effects of the wind turbine cut-in wind speed and acoustic deterrent were tested. The proposed structure of the randomized block design is depicted in Table 1. The analysis was proposed to be based on a generalized linear model with a normal error structure with a log-link.

2.3.1 Concerns of the peer review team that resulted in a change of approach to the first research study plan:

1. The appropriateness of the assumptions in the power analysis and how the analyses were implemented.

2. The peer review expressed concerns that the study plan blocks would be correlated, potentially violating ANOVA and ANODEV assumptions.

3. The peer review pointed that there could be a significant wind speed bias, as wind speeds increase.  Bats impacted by wind turbine blades during high wind speeds tend land further away from the base of the wind turbine.  This could result in an increased distribution bat carcasses landing outside the search zone, influencing the effectiveness comparison of curtailment versus the deterrent.

4. The peer review suggested a plot size bias due to an assumption that the bat deterrent does not protect the entire swept area of the rotor could result bat fatalities at the outer parameter of the rotor.  This assumption would lead one to the conclusion that bats struck at the outer perimeter of the wind turbine rotor swept area would tend, on average, to fall

farther from the turbine than those that are struck at random within the rotor swept area. However, examination of the spatial pattern of bat carcass recoveries at Cal Ridge carcass search study at the California Ridge Wind Farm in 2015, indicates a uniform distribution across 60-m radius plots.

Figure 1 - Plot of bat carcass recovery locations recorded across all plots and treatments for the 2015 Cal Ridge deterrent study

## **2.4 Second revision of the research study plan - Repeated measures design - utilizing a Generalized linear mixed effects (GLMM) model**

To attend to peer review concerns with the original research study plan, a second approach utilizing a repeated measures design was proposed in a significant revision to the original research study plan.  This revision allowed for a cost-effective increase in the number of searched wind turbines and increased searcher plot area on several sites to help provide insight to the wind speed bias concern.

The number of study wind turbines increased to 52.  The turbines would be selected from the 58wind turbine project with 40 wind turbines with 60-m plots and 12 wind turbines with 90-m plots and 38 days of searches with each day representing two days of mortality.  The change to a repeated measures design made it so that only 50% of the study turbines needed to be equipped with the bat deterrent system, resulting in only 26 wind turbines equipped, rather than the original proposed 40.  This resulted budget savings was planned to fund the additional bat fatality search on the larger plots.  It was determined that 12 90-m plots were feasible at the Orangeville project due to site landscape conditions, and 12 plots was the minimum necessary to calculate a variance.

A Generalized Linear Mixed Effects Model (GLMM) was proposed to evaluate the four treatments and two plot categories. Available turbines are randomly assigned to the four treatments in each plot configuration resulting in a sampling rate of 13 turbines per treatment, 10 per treatment for 60-m plot configurations (40 in total) and 3 per treatment for 90-m plot configurations (12 in total). The four treatments were defined as follows:

- 1) deterrent off, cut-in 3.5 m/s (control, CNDN),

- 2) deterrent on, cut-in 3.5 m/s (CNDY),

- 3) deterrent on, cut-in increased to 5.0 m/s (CYDY),

- 4) deterrent off, cut-in increased to 6.9 m/s (CYDN).

Carcass counts were planned to be conducted once every two days, for a two-day fatality assessment resulting in 38 counts per turbine over the season. The counts would be treated as repeated measures in the GLMM to separate within turbine variability from between turbine variability. Should day-to-day seasonal effects be seen as playing a role, the analysis was planned to be conducted using a Generalized Additive Mixed Effects Model (GAMM; Wood 2004; Harezlak, Ruppert, and Wand 2018), where the additive component could be used to represent nonparametrically estimated smoothed trends throughout the season across all turbines.  The generalized model framework allowed for characterization using alternative exponential family distributional assumptions, including a Poisson distribution for random events with mean counts near zero and a Quasi-Poisson distribution (in case of overdispersion) in addition to the standard Gaussian (Normal) distribution. This improved statistical approach represents fatality counts at low levels, with less bias than traditional Gaussian ANOVA methods would allow. The four treatments would contrast the effectiveness of different deterrent and turbine wind speed cut-in combinations compared to each other and compared to a control, consistent with the stated study goals.

Test of the hypotheses would be performed using approximate Chi-squared tests at α = 0.05. The appropriate one-tailed or two-tailed tests of treatments would be performed as dictated by the nature of the contrast being tested. Further, the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) would be used to rank models to assess goodness of fit in a likelihood context while accounting for differences in degrees of freedom. A total of 38 two-day areal assessment sweeps would be performed for each turbine between mid-July and the end of September. Under the simplest characterization of the experiment (i.e., combining treatments across plot configuration and without modeling seasonal trend) a total of 13 x 4 = 52 cumulative observations of bat mortality would be collected, the effects of acoustic deterrent and turbine cut-in wind speed can then be tested.  A simplified Analysis of Deviance (ANODEV; McCullagh and Nelder, 1999) degrees of freedom table for the proposed structure of the mixed effect design is depicted in Table 2.

Table 2 - Degree of freedom table for the proposed ANODEV of bat mortality estimates.

The analysis would be based on a generalized linear mixed effects model with Poisson error using a log-link. A log-link is considered appropriate due to anticipated deterrent effects would be proportional to the control conditions. Alternative considerations for error structure (e.g. QuasiPoisson) would depend on the distributional properties of the data collected.

## 2.4.1 Bat Behavioral Study

The original proposed study plan proposed approximately 40 wind turbines searching 60-m radius test plots, and early reviews by DOE suggested that 90-m plots were necessary to minimize an expected bias from the smaller, 60-m plots. As plot searches involve inspection of the entire searchable area of each test plot, the increased plot size caused a marked increase in program cost. To accommodate the additional expense of searching the additional 90-m plots within award funding, GE and DOE mutually agreed to remove the thermal imaging behavioral study from the program.  It was agreed that the four-treatment carcass study was more important to achieving the goals of the program than the thermal imaging behavioral study.  This change allowed budget for the statistical team to consider 12 90-m plots and 40 60-m plots in the simulations, numerous other plot configurations were considered.

## 2.4.2 Concerns of the peer review team that resulted in a change of approach to the second revision research study plan:

1. The prevailing concern had to do with the interaction of treatment, wind speed and detection probability (the fraction of carcasses falling outside plot boundaries). The reviewers continued to be concerned that the higher cut-in treatments, especially the 6.9 m/s cut-in, would bias the study because bats struck at high wind speeds would disproportionately fall outside 60-m and 90-m radius searcher plot size.  GE evaluated many options for sampling out to 90-m and even 120-m radius from the wind turbine, attempting to develop a cost-effective solution to address this concern.  In these scenarios, costs exceeded the budget well over twice the funding levels.

2. The peer review team raised a concern on the appropriateness of the assumptions that were made and how the analyses were implemented.  The initial assumptions of the power analysis raised concerns since it demonstrated decreasing power with increasing sample size, upon a revision of assumptions, the analyses failed to find sufficient power.

These concerns demonstrated that the team did not have enough wind statistical experience to fully understand the assumptions desired by the peer reviewers to obtain a rigorous research study plan.  As a result, the DOE supported augmentation of a person with wind wildlife statistician experience to the GE team, to help establish appropriate implementation and assumptions in the research study plan.

## **2.5 Third revision - Repeated measures design with wind turbines randomized across treatment and plot size configuration with binning of wind speeds, plus a direct comparison of repeated measures to random block designs**

Dr. Leslie New of Washington State University joined the GE team to support the third effort in the evolution of the research study plan.  Efforts were conducted to mitigate peer review concerns by optimizing the number of plots, plot sizes, number of search days, statistical assumptions, and analysis methods.  From February through May 2021, Dr. Sullivan and Dr. New, worked to determine the smallest sample size that is suitable to detect an effect at a level of significance suitable to pass a peer review.

To understand the optimal method for the proposed treatment plan, Dr. Leslie New with the support of Jeffery Mintz conducted a comparison study of repeated measures to random block designs.  Appendix A:  Power Analysis, details the comparison.

## 2.5.1 Carcass Study Simulation

Utilizing the statistical computing and graphics program R, the statistical team performed a simulation study to predict the number of bat carcasses expected from each of the treatments during the field study. Comparisons of simulated number of bat carcasses from each treatment provided a preview of the expected outcome of the field experiment. Statistical tests were performed to determine if differences in the number of bat carcasses would be significant (i.e., the study would likely have sufficient power to detect differences among treatments).  The statistical team first focused on a four-treatment study as was proposed in GE’s Technical Proposal in the Statement of Project Objectives (SOPO).

The budget for this study was developed for GE’s original proposal in response to the FOA. As the statistical team evaluated various scenarios to address peer reviewer concerns and develop a study plan, this budget ceiling was observed.

Initial simulations that incorporated the three wind-speed bins indicated that it may be possible to have sufficient power to detect a difference in the treatments of interest. However, careful review of the code and assumptions led to the realization that the effect size that had been used in the second revision was incorrect, mistakenly including the effect of the deterrent combined with feathering, rather than the effect of the deterrent alone. Once this was corrected, the lower effect size, combined with the small sample size, resulted in their being insufficient power to detect the effect size of interest with a four-treatment study. As a result, the team evaluated ways to increase power, specifically by modifying the field study to increase the sample size by a) increasing the number of days in the study, b) increasing the number of turbines, c) increasing searcher efficiency, and/or d) increasing plot size, all which was evaluated as the simulation study was conducted, along with other possible modifications to stretch the budget or improve the study (Table 4). The study design modifications described in Table 4 were evaluated by GE for the express purpose of increasing the power of the study design and reaching desired program goals. None of the proposed modifications were submitted for a third peer review due to all study designs considered indicated low power to detect an effect of the desired size and/or the study cost was estimated to exceed many times the award budget.

## 2.5.2 Four Treatment Simulation Study

The final efforts with Dr. Leslie New and Dr. Patrick Sullivan focused on resolutions to the prevailing concern with the interaction of treatment, wind speed and detection probability (the fraction of carcasses falling outside plot boundaries). Two of the treatments defined in this study are dependent on wind speed: curtailment at 5m/s + the acoustic deterrent and curtailment at 6.9 m/s. Because wind speed determines whether treatments can be differentiated, three wind speed bins were added to the simulation study methodology. To increase the number of bat carcasses found, the simulation study increased the number of plots to the maximum available plots allowed at OWF to 52, of which, 12 plots were 90-m radius, and 40 plots were 60-m radius.

In the SOPO, four treatments were proposed:

1. deterrent off, cut-in 3.5 m/s, the control treatment (Ctrl),

2. deterrent on, cut-in 3.5 m/s, the deterrent treatment (D)

3. deterrent on, cut-in increased to 5.0 m/sec, the deterrent with 5 m/s curtailment treatment (D + C5)

4. deterrent off, cut-in increased to 6.9 m/s, the 6.9 m/s curtailment treatment (C6.9).

The team developed a method to bin the four treatments in to three wind speed bins for direct differentiation of the fatality rates within the proposed wind speed bins:

1. 0 to 5 m/s (Low Wind Speed)

2. 5 to 6.9 m/s (Medium Wind Speed)

3. > 6.9 m/s (High Wind Speed)

Binning by wind speed resulted in an experiment that was essentially a 12-way experiment (4 treatments x 3 wind speeds, as shown in Figure 2 and Table 5). At low wind speeds, control turbines would cause mortality, and deterrent turbines are expected to have a reduced rate of mortality compared to the control (as was observed at California Ridge; Romano et al. 2019). However, at low wind speeds, turbines slated for the two curtailment treatments would be feathered and not running, no mortality would be anticipated, and the two treatments would be indistinguishable (Figure 2). At medium wind speeds, three of the treatments would be active (control, deterrent, and deterrent plus a 5.0 m/s cut-in), but the latter two treatments would be indistinguishable. In the high wind speed bin, the two deterrent treatments would be indistinguishable, as would the control and 6.9 m/s cut-in treatment.  Due to several comparisons are indistinguishable, they can be eliminated from analysis work, thus reducing the study plan to 7 comparisons, as shown in Figure 2 and Table 5.

Figure 2 – Binning the Study into Three Wind Speed Ranges

In conclusion, two of the treatments, curtailment at 5 m/s and curtailment at 6.9 m/s depend on wind speed and are therefore outside of control due to the variability of windspeeds over a single night, and as a result, while a treatment may be assigned, it may not be actuated. For example, at wind speeds greater than 6.9 m/s all turbines would be operational (no curtailment), so only the control and deterrent treatments would be actuated. It is key to understand, the treatments depend on the average wind speed for the night and power to detect differences decreases as the treatments are binned by wind speed.

Based on the lack of power to detect a difference among the means for a two-treatment study, no simulations of possible three-treatment studies were conducted, since, by inference, those simulations would also indicate the inability to detect differences among treatments.

## 2.5.5 Third Study Revision Conclusion

In the third effort to evolve the research study plan, all attempts to optimize the statistical plan indicated that the original four-treatment study and any three-treatment studies would not have the statistical power to detect the effectiveness of any treatment.  A reduction to a two-treatment study would not meet the goals and objectives of the original funding announcement and would not compel wind operators to adopt the technology without a comparison the deterrent to wind turbine curtailment, as a result, the two treatment study was eliminated from consideration.

## **3 Departures from the Plan and Why**

The SOPO called for the submittal of a draft and peer reviewed final research study plan, to be approved by DOE within budget period 1.  With the support of a DOE hosted peer review, several concerns and questions were raised.  The statistical team worked with the peer reviewers with multiple iterations of simulation studies of the experimental system using the statistical program R to address the concerns. The results of the simulation study indicated that neither the original program with a four-treatment study, nor a modified program with a three-treatment study would have the statistical power to detect the expected effect size. The departure from the plan resulted in the decision by GE and DOE to mutually terminate the program, as a result, no research study plan was submitted.

## 3.1.1 Key conclusions, learnings, and application

Simulation studies indicated that the four-treatment study plan proposed in the approved SOPO and any three-treatment studies lacked the statistical power to detect the expected effect of the

treatment, and a two-treatment study would not meet the goals and objectives of set by the original DOE funding announcement. While the initial power analyses conducted by GE and provided in the first draft of the study plan indicated that the study would have sufficient power to detect differences among treatments, there were unresolved issues with this analysis so an alternate approach was taken. Alternate simulations, when using the correct estimated effect of the deterrent, found that when each treatment was binned into three wind speeds, as was explored in response to DOE peer review concerns, the simulations did not have sufficient power to detect a difference between the treatments. The small sample size, coupled with the observed effect of the deterrent, made obtaining sufficient power difficult. The team was unsuccessful to recover power by adjusting study parameters without exceeding the budget several times over.

Simulation studies indicated that treatments are affected by wind speeds, binning in increments of the wind turbine cut-in speeds under comparison helps define when a treatment is actuated. Currently, there are no reliable methods of determining the wind speed at which each bat mortality occurs, at present, binning by nightly average wind speed is the most readily available approach to this issue.

In specific wind speed bins, certain treatments behave identically, and thus, the number of expected bat carcasses could be combined to increase experimental power. Under this experiment plan, each of the four treatments are separated into three wind speed bins.  This allows for 7 comparisons, as shown in Figure 2, Table 5, and Table 6.  Even with the simplification of comparisons, from 18 comparisons in Table 5 to 7 comparisons in Table 6, the number of bat carcasses in any comparison set is small and experimental power is low. Table 6 shows the comparisons that were analyzed, and while the simulations indicated that they did not provide the power sought, the approach might be successful at other sites where a larger sample size is possible.

A key takeaway from this study is the close attention needed when completing a power analysis, given not only the factors known to influence power (sample size, effect size), but also many of the subtleties and complications associated with bat interactions with wind facilities. When comparing bat fatality reduction strategies such as wind turbine curtailment at multiple wind speeds to a deterrent technology, the potential of the interaction between treatments requires a level of planning that is very robust and considers the extensive costs to obtain a sample size that can measure a desired difference between the treatments.

There are other considerations, such as the high level of variability in bat fatalities at a facility from year to year. This requires that attention be paid not only to the variability in the expected number of fatalities, as was done in this study through the simulation-based approach, but also potential unaccounted variation in the effectiveness of the deterrent, which often comes from only one or two seasons of study. Due to wind speed variation, the lack of control over the actuation of curtailment treatments, the complications of accounting for missed and scavenged carcasses, and many aspects unique to the deterrents being tested at any given wind facility means that the straightforward power analyses that are used for experimental designs in controlled settings are not truly appropriate for a wind farm, requiring deeper consideration of the power analysis.

## **5.1 Introduction**

The purpose of this exercise was to evaluate the statistical power of two study designs, repeated measures and a randomized block repeated measures design, to be able to evaluate the efficacy of three treatments intended to reduce bat fatalities at terrestrial wind facilities. In this appendix we describe the study designs and simulations used to estimate power, and present the results of the simulation along with our conclusions relative to the study’s objectives. The conceptual model of the relationship of treatments to wind speed, the definition of relevant contrasts and the structure of the simulation for estimating statistical power were developed by Manuela Huso (pers. comm.). It should be noted that a number of assumptions were made regarding a number of inputs to the model, including the distribution of wind speeds and expected mortalities, that are not reflective of the data from the proposed site for the experiment. Therefore, the results serve to show general patterns in the power of the two potential study designs, as opposed to reflecting the actual power of the proposed experiment.

There are four treatments being considered as part of this study, the control ( _O_ ) _,_ deterrent ( _D_ ), curtailment at 5 m/s plus the deterrent when the turbine is active ( _D5_ ), and curtailment at 6.9 m/s ( _C7_ ). On any given night of the experiment, the average wind speed ( W ) conditions can fall into one of three categories, _Low_ (  < 5 m/sW ), _Medium_ ( 5 m/s ≤ W<  6.9 m/s ) or _High_ ( W ≥ 6.9 m/s ). For the purpose of our simulation, we will be assuming that these wind speed categories occur with equal probability (i.e., 1/3 of the time each). Because two of the treatments are dependent on wind speed, these wind speed bins determine whether treatments can be differentiated. In the _Low_ category, _O_ is expected to cause mortality, and _D_ is expected to have a reduced rate of mortality compared to _O_ , but neither _D5_ or _C7_ will be running, resulting in an expected mortality rate of approximately zero for these two treatments and making _D5_ and _C7_ indistinguishable from one another. At _Medium_ wind speeds, the _D5_ turbines will be operating with the deterrent in place, making it equivalent to the _D_ turbines. Lastly, when average wind speed for a night is _High_ , _D_ and _D5_ will both be operating with the same expected reduction in mortality rate, while _C7_ turbines will be operating and therefore indistinguishable from _O_ . ## **5.2 Study Design**

Two study designs are being considered for this experiment, 1) repeated measures (RM) in which treatments are randomly assigned to a turbine at the start of the experiment and never change, and a 2) randomized block repeated measures design (RBD), in which the turbine is considered the block and treatments are assigned such that on any given night, each treatment is assigned to a quarter of the turbines and each turbine receives each treatment an equal number of times. Within both the RM and RBD designs we group the counts within each wind speed bin, so that each turbine will have a single count of total observed fatalities per wind speed category – treatment combination. For the RM design, this means there will be three measurements per turbine, one for each wind speed category, while for the RBD there will be 12 measurements per turbine, one for each of the four treatments in each of the three wind speed categories.

One of the difficulties of this experiment is that two of the treatments, curtailment at 5 m/s and curtailment at 6.9 m/s depend on wind speed and are therefore outside of our control. As a result, while a treatment may be assigned, that is not the same as treatment actuation. For example, at wind speeds greater than 6.9 m/s all turbines will be operational, so only the deterrent treatment will be actuated. This places a constraint on the study in that the treatments have different meaning depending on the average wind speed for the night. It also potentially creates difficulties, since there is the potential for an unbalanced study design, with treatments being allocated equally, but potentially not being actuated for all turbines. This may pose a particular problem if the wind speed categories do not occur with equal probability.

The analysis for both study designs was written as a Poisson GLMM, with wind speed category, treatment and a wind speed category-by-treatment interaction. The RM design includes turbine as a random effect and an offset equal to the number of nights in each wind speed category. The RBD includes turbine and a turbine-by-treatment interaction term as random effects and an offset equal to the number of nights in each wind speed category – treatment combination.

## **5.4 Simulation Algorithm**

For each Design scenario (Table 9), Repeat steps 1-6 1000 times:

1. Generate the mean mortality rate per turbine, λλii and seasonal adjusted mortality, λλ′i .

2. Generate MMi∗ , the fatalities that would be realized under normal turbine operation.

3. Generate MMi , the actual fatalities given wind speed conditions and assigned treatment. Treatment assignment will differ between RBD and RM, hence, so will mortality.

4. Generate AAi , the animals which fall within the search area for the given search radius and windspeed, as specified by _RE_ .

5. Generate XXi , the observed fatalities based on MMi , with probability of detection based on searcher efficiency (dog-handlers).

6. Fit generalized linear mixed effects model appropriate to design.

7. Save contrast estimates for RM and RBD separately.

Our power to detect differences between two treatments is measured by the proportion of times across 1000 iterations that we detect that a contrast between the treatment means is significant. A significant contrast is a contrast unlikely to have been zero given the observations, as measured by whether the contrast’s 95% confidence interval contains zero.  The power under a given study design is the proportion of the trials for which the study produced a significant contrast.  Of interest as well is whether there is any bias in our estimates of the treatment contrasts. We know the expected value of each contrast, _E[contrast],_ because we fixed values of _E_ and _RE_ , the effects we are trying to detect. We summarized this bias as the ratio of the estimated contrast exp [m m (c mmc mmc )] log2 , where _log2(E[contrast])_ was based upon the values in the matrix _E_ and ~~~~ EE[c mmc mmc ]  _mean_ ( _contrast_ ) was calculated on the log scale (given the Poisson distribution with the log link).

## **5.6 Conclusions**

There is notable bias in the estimate of contrasts conditioned on wind speed based on the search radius (Figure 4 and Figure 5), with the between radius variance in bias being greater than the within radius variance in bias. Given the improved power to detect differences in the contrasts with the larger sample size in terms of the number of turbines, we would recommend a study design that maximizes the number of turbines searched, while still allowing for a sufficient number of search nights to allow for the sample to be representative of the study period. The RBD gives better power to detect the effect of the deterrent to the control, which is the purpose of this study, and has equal power to detect the other contrasts of interest (although with large bias) when compared with the RM design. However, to implement the RBD, the deterrent would need to be installed on all turbines in the study, which would in turn limit the number of turbines that could be included (due the additional expense), and thus may ultimately reduce the power compared to an RM design with a larger number of turbines. As a result, for a fixed budget, the choice of study design ultimately comes down to which maximizes power, minimizes bias and meets the budgetary and logistical constraints.
